chapter: Trio, Eckstine accompanist and Illinois Jacquet, 1945-48
title: The Benny Carter school of musicianship
summary: Players who worked for Benny Carter, such as Dizzy, Max Roach and J.J., learned proper section playing and intonation.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: There's something about certain musicians that I have noticed, and most of them, whenever you mention it or talk about it... There are certain schools of music or certain bandleaders that guys have been with that, when they come out of that particular school, they have a real extra thing about

musicianship. This particular leader that I'm talking about happened to be Benny Carter. Benny Carter, and any musician will tell you this that ever worked with him... And I've never met Benny Carter personally, but I've always admired him since I first heard him back in the Thirties. Any musician that has worked with him will tell you that when you're with Benny Carter, you're in school, and you learn to play properly and good, or else you don't stay there. And I've heard this from Dizzy Gillespie, I've heard it from Max Roach, I've heard it from J.J. Johnson, and any number of other people that I can't think of right now. And every one of them are excellent musicians, you know, when it comes to playing section or whatever -- but mainly section.... And reading and, you know, playing proper. Benny Carter was.... Any band that he ever had, even if the band wasn't a hard-swinging band or anything, it always had very good intonation and it always had, you know... They always played together in every respect, you know...
So J.J. Johnson was just one of those excellent musicians, with talent and he had that seriousness about him about music, that was unparalleled, so to speak.
